assessment.nobel_worthiness: A new topological classification of electronic states, predicted by theory (Z2 invariant, spin-orbit-driven quantum spin Hall state) and then seen in HgTe wells, with an extension to 3D materials. It is a new quantum state of matter with robust edge transport and lasting reach across condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the decisive theory, and Molenkamp's group the first experimental confirmation. Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction and Zhang's role are outside the supplied credit, which is a known allocation problem; the three supplied names form a clean prize configuration.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed in many materials and by ARPES and transport; the concept is stable and well understood theoretically with first-principles support. Recognition is timely or overdue.
uncertainties: The BHZ prediction for HgTe lies outside the credited names, so credit could be contested.
I rely on memory of the history and have not verified details independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Prediction of flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene, followed by observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity. It opened moire quantum matter as a tunable platform for strong correlations, a surprise of the kind I value.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the continuum-model prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experiments. Cao and Fatemi, first authors, and other groups are not credited, and an allocation of three is delicate.
assessment.maturity: Observations have been reproduced widely since 2018, but the nature of the superconductivity and correlated states is still debated. The field is young, so recognition is somewhat early, though the core prediction-plus-experiment is solid.
uncertainties: Mechanism of the superconductivity remains unsettled.
Sample-dependent behaviour and reproducibility between devices.
Fairness of excluding the first authors of the experiments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: DMFT is the standard non-perturbative framework for strongly correlated materials and, combined with DFT, a quantitative route to spectra of real compounds (Mott transition, heavy fermions, transition-metal oxides). It is conceptually original and has enormous methodological impact.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimensional limit, and Georges and Kotliar developed the mapping to an impurity model and the exact formulation. Credit among Metzner, Vollhardt, Georges, Kotliar and Rozenberg is intricate, and a fair trio is arguable with the names supplied.
assessment.maturity: Several decades of use and validation against photoemission and optical data, with strong agreement in many cases and known limits (non-local correlations). The work is mature, though it is a method as much as a discovery.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee views it as a discovery or as a computational method.
Metzner is not in the credited names, which affects fairness.
Quantitative predictive power for complex materials varies.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Giant tunnel magnetoresistance in epitaxial MgO junctions came from a theory prediction of coherent spin-dependent tunnelling, then realisation at room temperature. It underlies hard-disk read heads and MRAM, which is practical impact tied to clear physics, and electronic-structure theory was decisive.
assessment.attribution: Butler's first-principles calculation, and the Parkin and Yuasa experiments of 2004, gave the core result. Mathon and Umerski, and Djayaprawira and others, also made contributions, so the three-way split is not unique.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by two groups at the same time, commercialised for over a decade, and the interpretation is stable. It is strongly mature, though the Nobel prize in 2007 already honoured GMR, so proximity to prior recognition counts.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2007 GMR prize in the minds of some members.
Simultaneous independent discoveries and the Mathon-Umerski theory credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED gave strong coupling of microwave photons to superconducting qubits and made a platform for dispersive readout and gates, the basis of most superconducting quantum processors. The 2025 prize was for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, so this follows naturally, though the committee must avoid appearing repetitive.
assessment.attribution: Blais with Girvin and Huang proposed the architecture, and the Wallraff and Schoelkopf group showed strong coupling in 2004. Girvin is not in the credited names, a notable gap in attribution.
assessment.maturity: Broadly confirmed, and the technology is advancing strongly. Basic science is mature, while the largest consequences lie ahead, so recognition is plausibly timely but could be premature to some.
uncertainties: Close in subject to the 2025 prize.
Exclusion of Girvin and Huang from the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks use magic-wavelength trapping to reach about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, enabling tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. It is original and has clear, lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock and Ye's group reached the leading precision and many-body clock physics. Single-ion clock work and the comb contributions are outside this candidate.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by several laboratories worldwide. The Nobel prize in 2005 included the frequency comb, so partially adjacent. Recognition is timely, as the redefinition of the second is under discussion.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 comb prize and ion-clock work (Wineland 2012).
Reach beyond metrology is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold fermions and bosons in optical lattices realise Hubbard models with tunable parameters, giving a quantum simulator for correlated matter, including Mott insulators and antiferromagnetic correlations. It relates directly to the problems of correlated electrons I care about.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch proposed it, Greiner and Bloch the Mott transition experiment, and Esslinger the fermionic Mott insulator. Jaksch is not in the supplied names, and Greiner makes four plausible people for three places.
assessment.maturity: The experiments are mature and replicated, and microscopes now show spin correlations. Whether it has solved an open materials problem, such as d-wave pairing in Hubbard models, is not yet settled, so the impact is not yet complete.
uncertainties: Genuine quantum advantage over classical Hubbard simulation not demonstrated.
Overlap with earlier cold-atom prizes (1997, 2001) and unsettled credit split.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetically driven ferroelectricity (TbMnO3 and related compounds) and strong magnetoelectric coupling showed a new mechanism for ferroelectricity and cross-control of order parameters. It is an important materials-physics result, with DFT insight into spin-orbit and exchange origins.
assessment.attribution: Kimura and Tokura found the first spiral-magnet ferroelectrics; Cheong made major contributions on multiferroic materials. Ramesh worked on BiFeO3 thin films, which is a distinct strand, so the compound discovery may need different recognition.
assessment.maturity: Widely confirmed and understood theoretically, but practical device use (voltage control of magnetism) has not yet been realised, so the impact is mostly academic so far.
uncertainties: Compound discovery with different parts and unresolved credit (Kimura, Spaldin, Ramesh).
